chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 201-220: short speeches of the love situations, waiting under the promised rains, the friend's comfort drawn from beasts on the man's road, and love argued as feast and as pain.

201.reading: The heroine blesses the woman next door, may she eat ambrosia, because she brought word that the lord of the hill land will come, the land of tall bamboo groves where a soft blue-winged, sharp-clawed creature that has eaten honey-sweet mango like mixed milk gulps sour nelli and hangs from the thornless bamboo nearby.
201.nuance: The blessing of food (அமிழ்தம் உண்க) repays the bearer of good news, as Kuruntokai 210 repays the crow; the creature that hangs from the bamboo is the bat. Its meal of the sweet and then the sour may be read as a hint of the hero's mixed dealings, but no second correspondence is anchored, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: bamboo groves and the hill-land lord fix the hills

comparisons.tenor: the honey-sweet mango, sweet as milk mixed (with honey)

202.reading: The heroine tells her aching heart that, as the small-leaved nerunji thick on poor ground first gives a new flower sweet to the eye and then bears thorns, her lover who once did sweet things now does cruel ones.
202.nuance: The refrain நோம் என் நெஞ்சே opens and closes the poem, so the simile sits inside the pain; the point of the nerunji is the order of its gifts, flower first and thorn after, which turns the comparison into a story of a love.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's turn from kindness to hurt is the household grievance of marutham

comparisons.tenor: the lover who did sweet things and now does painful ones

203.reading: The heroine says her man is not from a land beyond the hills nor from a town too far to see its treetops; he lives within sight, yet keeps apart from her like those who have gone over to the god, and once she would not have grieved for him so.
203.nuance: The two negations measure distance by what can be seen (hills between, treetops out of sight), so the pain is a nearness without contact; the simile of those who have reached the god makes his avoidance a kind of vow. The last line's மன் gives a past that is lost: before, she had no cause to pine.

thinai_evidence.note: he lives in the same town yet keeps away, the marutham estrangement

comparisons.tenor: the man who lives near but keeps apart from her

204.reading: The companion tells the broad-shouldered hero that people cry 'love, love', but love is neither a possessing spirit nor a disease: think of it, and it is like an old cow nibbling the young unripe grass that has sprung on old upland, a feast always new.
204.nuance: The old cow can only lick at grass too short to graze, and gets pleasure without fullness; so the companion's 'feast' (விருந்து) is also a gentle deflation of the hero's suffering. அணங்கு and பிணி name exactly the two explanations, spirit and sickness, that akam poems give for a lover's state.

thinai_evidence.note: the companion answers the hero's lovesickness in the secret stage

comparisons.vehicle: முதைச்சுவற் கலித்த முற்றா இளம்புல் மூதா தைவந்
comparisons.tenor: love, a pleasure ever new that never fills

205.reading: The heroine asks her friend how the pallor spreading over her fragrant forehead came to know it so soon, when the lord of the heaped-sand shore has only now left, mounting his white chariot bright with gold, rising like sky-going swans under lightning-laden rain clouds, its wheels wet with spray from the churning sea.
205.nuance: The question gives the pallor a mind of its own (யாங்கு அறிந்தன்று), so the body knows the parting before she has taken it in; the white chariot rising like swans against dark rain cloud is the last thing she sees.

thinai_evidence.note: sea spray and the sand-shore lord fix the coast

comparisons.tenor: the white chariot rising away swiftly

206.reading: The hero says that if even the qualities of a woman so sweet, whose lovely words are like ambrosia, can bring such unbearable grief, love is hard to live with, and he warns the wise to keep from coming near it.
206.nuance: The argument runs from the best case: not a cruel woman but a sweet one causes the pain, so love itself is the cause. The plural அறிவுடையீர் may be his companions, which makes the poem a reply to counsel like the companion's in Kuruntokai 204.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero's lovesick grief before union is settled belongs to the secret stage

207.reading: The heroine says many who love her told her he went without telling her, thinking that if he spoke the going would become hard, along the old narrow path beside the rocky hill, printing his fine footsteps, where the clear lonely cry of a kite parted from its flock, perched in the fork of a dry omai, is the only companion in grief for those who cross the wasteland.
207.nuance: She knows the road only by report, yet she pictures his footprints on it; the kite separated from its kind is a companion to the traveller, which may hint that he too is now alone, but the bird only cries, so it carries a mood and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the wasteland road and the dry omai of the waste

208.reading: The heroine tells her friend she is not one who will refuse: she will be one with the lord of the land where the vengai, its trunk crushed by fighting elephants, blooms low enough for the hill women to pluck its flowers standing, for their hair; with anyone else she will not be one.
208.nuance: The poem turns on ஒன்று, to be one, to agree, in five forms; the last line can be read as refusing another match the family proposes. The crushed vengai that blooms within reach can be taken as the heroine, hurt but still giving, but only one pair can be anchored, so it is a near miss and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill, the vengai and the hill people's women

209.reading: The hero, having crossed the hard hill where green nelli lies on the path and the tiger cub's kill-ground roars, says he does not count the many short steps (of the way), for he carries the love of the young woman whose dark thick hair smells of the many opening buds of the bent-branched vetchi growing in the forest at the path's edge.
209.nuance: The sense of குறுநடை பல உள்ளலமே is unsettled: it may be that he does not think of the short stages of the road, or of her short-stepped walk; அறந்தலைப் பட்ட may mean the nelli has become a charity for travellers. The vetchi at the path's edge brings her scent into the wilderness.

thinai_evidence.note: the man speaks after crossing the hard way, away from her

210.reading: The friend tells the returned hero that even if she offered in seven bowls hot white rice grown entire in Thondi with ghee from the many cows of the herdsmen of Nalli's forest, Nalli of the strong chariot, it would be little as the offering due to the crow that cawed to bring a guest and so ended the grief that wasted her friend's broad shoulders.
210.nuance: The guest the crow called is the husband himself, now at the door, so the thanks to the bird is praise of his return said to his face. The meal is priced by the two most famous sources of plenty the poet knows, Nalli's herds and Thondi's rice; the poet's name, Kakkai Padiniyar, comes from this poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsmen and their cows of the forest pasture

211.reading: The friend tells the heroine that they have stopped fearing for the man who, unkind, agreed to leave her as her chosen bangles slipped, and crossed the waterless wasteland where a bee, sucking honey from the single summer cluster on the hot bough of a scorched kadamba, goes away unsatisfied.
211.nuance: அஞ்சல் எஞ்சினம் is bitter: they have given up even fearing for him. The bee that leaves the one cluster on a burnt tree still hungry is what he has chosen over her full love.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless waste and the scorched tree

iraicchi.act: the bee sucks at the one cluster left on a scorched tree and goes away unsated
iraicchi.sense: the man who left her full love has gone where nothing can satisfy him, so his leaving gains him nothing

212.reading: The friend says the long chariot with curved rail that the lord of the shore drives comes, its clear bells ringing on the shore of the clear sea, only to be seen and then goes back leaving shame; pitiable is such love, it will surely die, and she grieves.
212.nuance: காண வந்து நாணப் பெயரும்: the visit gives sight and then shame, and nothing lasting; the friend's grief is a push toward marriage, since a love that only shows itself is one that will fade.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore and its lord

213.reading: The friend tells the heroine that the man has deep love for them, since on the road taken by those who spurned their sweet sleep, they say, the old fork-horned stag pulls down with its foot the big dry leaves bent low and eats only if (its mate and young) leave any, and failing that stands as shade for its fawn and lets the sun pass.
213.nuance: The words of lines 3 to 5 (ததரல், தெறித்து நடை மரபின்) are hard, and who leaves food for whom is not certain; the sense of a stag starving to shelter its young is clear. என்ப makes it hearsay of the road, which is how the friend can promise what he must have seen.

thinai_evidence.note: the stag sheltering its young from the sun on the wasteland road

iraicchi.act: the stag eats only what is left and stands as shade over its young in the sun
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees such care on his road will remember his own and come back to shelter her

214.reading: The friend says this noisy town has been thrown into confusion since the hill girl of soft gait and lovely hair down her back, who guards the shining-eared millet the forest man sowed after clearing his plot, was given a great leaf skirt for her jewelled waist, stripping the asoka to its trunk, and crowned with a garland of the arali that grows nearby.
214.nuance: The stripped asoka is the evidence: a gift that took a whole tree cannot be hidden, and the town reads it. ஏமுற்றன்று may also mean the town is deluded, taking the signs for a god's possession; the subject of the giving is not named, and the reading of the confusion is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarded by the hill girl in the forest man's plot

215.reading: As grief spreads and the sun slowly withdraws to hide behind the great hill of summer, the friend asks whether he will come today, he who crossed the wasteland by the tall mountain where the elephant with crossed tusks, having searched the dry pool, embraces his beloved mate beside the low rock while the great striped tiger lies in wait.
215.nuance: The sunset and the question 'will he come today' make it an evening of waiting; the tiger that 'guards' the elephants is a watcher of prey, so the road is both a picture of faithful pairs and a danger to him.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer heat and the crossed wasteland

iraicchi.act: the elephant, finding the pool dry, holds close to its mate on the hillside
iraicchi.sense: even in drought and danger the beast keeps to its mate, so the man who sees it will turn back to her

216.reading: The heroine says he has crossed the forest of green-leaved, never-wilting valli to bring flawless wealth, while she, her rows of bright bangles slipping, has sighed and sunk in grief on the bed made for sleep; and the great cloud, without saying 'she is pitiable', still pours, thunders and flashes, friend, with her sweet life as its aim.
216.nuance: அவரே and யானே set the two halves against each other, his errand and her bed; the rain, the season he named, comes as an attacker rather than a promise. The poem is spoken under the rains, so the waiting is mullai though the colophon files it under the journey.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain of the season he named has come and she waits

217.reading: The friend says she told the hill lord that if they were sent to drive parrots from the millet they could meet by day, but she feared his coming by night, and asked what they could do for their trouble; he took all she said for something else and surely sighed; love is delicate, and she had spoken only of great prudence and of blame.
217.nuance: She proposes the day tryst for safety and he hears a refusal; ஐதே காமம் admits how easily a word can wound it. The last line is hard: முதுக்குறைமை is mature prudence, and she may mean the girl's or her own.

thinai_evidence.note: guarding millet from parrots, and the hill lord

218.reading: The heroine says that she will make vows to the victorious goddess of the cleft hill caves, tie the sacred thread on her wrist, heed the birds and stand for chance words, and still think of him, friend, since he is like life to her life, he who once could not bear to be parted even for a blink and now can forget her and stay away.
218.nuance: The list of rites is everything a woman could do to bring him back, and it closes on the one she cannot stop, thinking of him. The contrast is inside his own past: the man for whom a blink was too long a parting is the one who can now stay away.

thinai_evidence.note: he stays far off, forgetting her

comparisons.tenor: the man, dear to her as life to her life

219.reading: The heroine says her body is pale, her longing is with the unkind-hearted man, her restraint has gone far off, and her mind keeps saying 'rise, let us go to him', saying what cannot be done; but there will be no place for her, friend, with the lord of the shore of thorny-leaved broad-trunked screwpine, if he asks 'and who are you?'
219.nuance: Each part of her is somewhere else (pallor on the body, longing with him, restraint far away, reason urging her out); the only thing that holds her is the fear of being met as a stranger. The phrasing of line 7 is restored from Swaminatha Aiyar's text and its sense is not settled.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine shore and its lord

220.reading: The heroine tells her friend to see: in the woodland of fragrant flowers, where the stag has cropped the new varagu sprung from the old rain to stubble and the jasmine blooming by the straw has loosened its small buds like a wild cat smiling, even the evening ringed with bees has come and those who left for wealth have not.
220.nuance: The varagu has been sown, grown and cropped since he left, so the scene is a clock of the seasons; the jasmine buds opening like a wild cat's bared teeth make the promised season's smile a sneer.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening in the jasmine woodland after the rains

links.note: Kuruntokai 202 sets the nerunji's flower, sweet to the eye, before its thorn as the lover's kindness before his cruelty; Kural 1120 uses only the nerunji fruit, the thorn, to say how soft things feel to her feet.
links.teaches: Both poets know the nerunji as a plant that pleases first and pricks after; the couplet takes only the prick to praise a woman's delicacy, while the Sangam poem uses the order of flower and thorn to tell the history of a love, so the same plant can measure a body or a story.

links.note: Kuruntokai 204: the companion says love is neither a spirit nor a disease but a feast always new; 206: the hero says love brings unbearable grief and warns the wise to keep away.
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems are the two sides of the companion's rebuke and the hero's answer: the friend outside love calls it a light pleasure, and the man inside it calls it a pain the wise should flee, so the anthology lets each speaker's place decide what love is.

links.note: Kuruntokai 206 tells the wise to keep from love because the woman is too sweet, her words like ambrosia; Naladiyar 41 tells men to turn from desire because the admired body is a frail bag the crows would tear.
links.teaches: The same counsel, keep away from love, rests on opposite judgments of the beloved: the Sangam lover flees because she is ambrosia and the pain is love's own, the Jain moralist because she is carrion under skin, so the later ethic keeps the advice and reverses its reason.

links.note: Kural 1185: look there, my lover is going; look here, the pallor is spreading on my body. Kuruntokai 205 asks how the pallor on her forehead knew so soon, when the shore lord has only now driven away.
links.teaches: The couplet's two pointing words make his going and her paling one instant; the Kuruntokai poem has the same instant but turns it into a question to the pallor itself, and supplies the scene the couplet leaves out, the white chariot rising like swans and the sea spray on its wheels.

links.note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kuruntokai 207: he left without telling her, thinking that if he spoke, going would become hard, and she heard of it from others.
links.teaches: The couplet's demand to be told assumes the parting is spoken; the Kuruntokai man knows the power of that speech so well that he avoids it, so the heroine is denied even the chance to answer him that the Kural's speaker uses.

links.note: Purananuru 150: Nalli, unnamed, roasts fat in his forest for a starving poet and gives him his own chain. Kuruntokai 210: the friend prices the meal owed to the crow that called a guest in the ghee of the herds of Nalli's forest.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows why Nalli's forest is the measure in the love poem: he was remembered as the host who fed a stranger in the woods unasked, so the friend, repaying a bird for bringing a guest, reaches for the most famous hospitality she knows and still calls it too little.

links.note: Kuruntokai 213: the friend says he has deep love, since on his road the stag goes hungry and stands as shade for its young. Akananuru 59: the friend says on his road the bull elephant bends a tree so its mate can eat, yet those men do not remember her.
links.teaches: The same device, a beast caring for its own on the road the man took, is used for opposite ends: in Kuruntokai the friend makes it proof that he will come back, in the Akananuru she makes it the reproach that he does not, so the image does not carry its comfort in itself but takes it from the speaker's verdict.

links.note: Akananuru 34: the returning man sees a stag feed its doe and guard her sleep and bids his charioteer hurry home. Kuruntokai 213: the friend says that on his road, they say, the stag starves to shelter its young, so he has deep love.
links.teaches: The friend's comfort in Kuruntokai is a prediction that the man will see the beasts' care and be moved; Akananuru 34 shows that very sight working on the man himself, so the two poems give the two ends of one iraicchi, the promise at home and its fulfilment on the road.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 1: the friend says the man who promised to come when the rain hung low can hardly fail to come now that the clouds roar and pour. Kuruntokai 216: the heroine says the great cloud pours, thunders and flashes with no pity, aimed at her life.
links.teaches: The rain of the promised season is the same sign in both, but the friend reads it as his oath falling due and the heroine as the deadline passing on her; set side by side, the poems show the rainy season carries both senses at once, and the speaker decides which is heard.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 3: the friend, showing her own distress, says the wind, hail and thundering sky act as if all aimed at one lone woman. Kuruntokai 216: the heroine says the thundering cloud flashes with her life as its aim.
links.teaches: The complaint that the storm is aimed at her is the heroine's own in the older poem, and in the later venba the friend speaks it for her about 'one woman', so the charge against the rain had become a formula that could be handed from the sufferer to her companion.

links.note: Kural 1209: her life is ending as she thinks of the unkindness of one who said they were not separate. Kuruntokai 218: he, like life to her life, who could not bear a parting even a blink long, can now forget her and stay away, and she will still think of him.
links.teaches: The couplet names the wound as the broken claim of oneness; the Kuruntokai poem gives the claim its measure, not a blink apart, and adds what the woman does with the wound, vows, omens and thought, so the poem shows the couplet's dying as a life kept busy with ritual.

links.note: Kural 1255: the dignity of not going after one who has turned away is unknown to those sick with love. Kuruntokai 219: her restraint has gone far and her mind urges her to go to him, but she holds back for fear he will ask 'who are you?'
links.teaches: The couplet says the lovesick cannot know the pride of not following; the Kuruntokai heroine, lovesick, still stays, held back not by pride but by fear of being met as a stranger, so the poem shows a restraint that survives the loss of honour and the couplet's claim is too absolute.

links.note: Kural 1227: this sickness buds in the morning, swells through the day and blossoms in the evening. Kuruntokai 220: in the evening the jasmine opens its small buds like a wild cat smiling, and the man who left for wealth has not come.
links.teaches: The couplet makes a flower's day the shape of love-sickness; the Kuruntokai poem shows the real flower, the mullai opening its buds at dusk in the season he named, at the moment her grief opens, so the metaphor rests on the evening flowering of the jasmine land.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 14: the friend says they are sure he will come quickly, since the rain cloud laughs softly as the mullai shows its bright teeth. Kuruntokai 220: the jasmine buds open like a wild cat smiling, the evening is here, and he has not come.
links.teaches: Both poems read the opening jasmine as a smile with teeth, but in the friend's venba it is the season laughing in welcome and in the heroine's Kuruntokai poem it is a wild cat's grin, so the one image turns from promise to mockery once the day of return has passed.

source_issues: 201 to 220: the colophon thurai names only the speaker (தலைவி கூற்று and the like), so thurai_akam occasion words are null and addressees are inferred from the poems.
209 line 1: அறந்தலைப் பட்ட and line 4 குறுநடை பல உள்ளலமே are hard to construe; the reading is marked uncertain.
213 lines 3 to 5: ததரல் and தெறித்துநடை மரபின் are rare, and who leaves food for whom is unclear; marked uncertain.
219 line 7: our text was replaced by the tamilvu (Swaminatha Aiyar) reading; the phrase எந் நீரிரோ is construed as 'who are you?', which is uncertain.
216: our thinai (mullai, from the rains) differs from the colophon's paalai.
